title: Economics syllabus flashcards
format_note: Each clashcard has a context-specific front and a short, accurate definition as the back.
source_note: Cards are based on the visible 'Suggested concepts' boxes in the uploaded 4-page syllabus excerpt. Terms visibly crossed out in the source are included and marked as 'crossed_out_in_source'.

clashcards.front: D1 Market structures — perfect vs. imperfect competition
clashcards.back: Perfect competition has many firms and no market power; imperfect competition gives firms some market power.

clashcards.front: D1 Market structures — market forms
clashcards.back: Different structures of markets, such as perfect competition, monopoly, oligopoly and monopolistic competition.

clashcards.front: D1 Market structures — economic models vs. real markets
clashcards.back: Models simplify reality; real markets usually do not fully match model assumptions.

clashcards.front: D1 Market structures — characteristics / conditions
clashcards.back: The features needed for a market structure, such as number of firms, barriers and product type.

clashcards.front: D1 Market structures — assumptions
clashcards.back: Simplifying ideas used to build an economic model, for example perfect information or rational behaviour.

clashcards.front: D1 Market structures — infinite number of firms
clashcards.back: In perfect competition, there are so many small firms that no single firm can influence price.

clashcards.front: D1 Market structures — market power
clashcards.back: In perfect competition, firms have no market power and must accept the market price.

clashcards.front: D1 Market structures — price taker
clashcards.back: A firm that accepts the market price because it is too small to influence it.

clashcards.front: D1 Market structures — price maker
clashcards.back: A firm able to influence price; in perfect competition firms are not price makers.

clashcards.front: D1 Market structures — identical / homogeneous product
clashcards.back: All firms sell the same product, so consumers see no difference between suppliers.

clashcards.front: D1 Market structures — barriers to entry and exit
clashcards.back: In perfect competition, firms can enter or leave the market freely and cheaply.

clashcards.front: D1 Market structures — allocative efficiency
clashcards.back: Resources are allocated so that price equals marginal cost, maximizing social welfare.

clashcards.front: D1 Market structures — externalities
clashcards.back: Costs or benefits affecting third parties; they can stop even competitive markets being socially efficient.

clashcards.front: D1 Market structures — supernormal profits competed away
clashcards.back: In the long run, new firms enter and reduce profits until only normal profit remains.

clashcards.front: D1 Market structures — equilibrium positions
clashcards.back: Market outcomes where demand equals supply and firms have no incentive to change output.

clashcards.front: D1 Market structures — long-run normal profit
clashcards.back: In perfect competition, firms earn just enough profit to keep resources in the industry.

clashcards.front: D1 Market structures — productive efficiency
clashcards.back: Production occurs at the lowest possible average cost.

clashcards.front: D1 Market structures — government competition policies
clashcards.back: Policies used to maintain fair competition and prevent excessive market power.

clashcards.front: D1 Market structures — single seller
clashcards.back: A monopoly market has one dominant seller supplying the product.

clashcards.front: D1 Market structures — pure monopoly
clashcards.back: A market structure with only one firm and no close substitutes.

clashcards.front: D1 Market structures — market share
clashcards.back: The percentage of total market sales controlled by one firm.

clashcards.front: D1 Market structures — monopoly power
clashcards.back: The ability of a firm to influence price because it faces little or no competition.

clashcards.front: D1 Market structures — competitors
clashcards.back: Other firms in the market; in monopoly, competitors are absent or weak.

clashcards.front: D1 Market structures — price maker
clashcards.back: A monopolist can set or strongly influence price rather than accept the market price.

clashcards.front: D1 Market structures — barriers to entry
clashcards.back: Obstacles that stop new firms entering, such as patents, high costs or control of resources.

clashcards.front: D1 Market structures — advertising and product differentiation
clashcards.back: Methods monopolists use to strengthen brand image and reduce substitutability.

clashcards.front: D1 Market structures — consumer choice
clashcards.back: The range of options available to consumers; monopoly usually reduces choice.

clashcards.front: D1 Market structures — productive inefficiency
clashcards.back: A monopolist may not produce at the lowest average cost due to weak competition.

clashcards.front: D1 Market structures — allocative inefficiency
clashcards.back: A monopolist often restricts output and sets price above marginal cost.

clashcards.front: D1 Market structures — innovation
clashcards.back: Monopolies may innovate using large profits, but weak competition can also reduce pressure to innovate.

clashcards.front: D1 Market structures — x-inefficiency
clashcards.back: Costs are higher than necessary because lack of competition reduces pressure to be efficient.

clashcards.front: D1 Market structures — natural monopoly
clashcards.back: A market where one firm can supply the whole market more cheaply due to economies of scale.

clashcards.front: D1 Market structures — economies of scale
clashcards.back: Average costs fall as output rises, often strengthening monopoly power.

clashcards.front: D1 Market structures — innovative ideas
clashcards.back: New products, processes or methods that may be protected and used to gain market power.

clashcards.front: D1 Market structures — intellectual property rights
clashcards.back: Legal protection of ideas, designs or inventions, such as copyright and patents.

clashcards.front: D1 Market structures — copyright
clashcards.back: Legal protection for creative work that can act as a barrier to entry.

clashcards.front: D1 Market structures — patents
clashcards.back: Legal protection for inventions, giving temporary monopoly rights.

clashcards.front: D1 Market structures — protection
clashcards.back: Legal or market barriers that shield a firm from competitors.

clashcards.front: D1 Market structures — incentive
clashcards.back: A reason to act; monopoly profit can be an incentive to invest or innovate.

clashcards.front: D1 Market structures — risk
clashcards.back: The uncertainty a firm faces when investing, innovating or entering a market.

clashcards.front: D1 Market structures — price discrimination
clashcards.back: Charging different consumer groups different prices for the same product when possible.

clashcards.front: D1 Market structures — concentration ratio
clashcards.back: The share of market sales controlled by the largest firms in an oligopoly.

clashcards.front: D1 Market structures — domination
clashcards.back: A few large firms control most of the market.

clashcards.front: D1 Market structures — competition
clashcards.back: Firms rival each other through price, quality, advertising or innovation.

clashcards.front: D1 Market structures — collusion
clashcards.back: Firms cooperate to reduce competition, often by fixing prices or output.

clashcards.front: D1 Market structures — formal collusion
clashcards.back: Explicit agreement between firms, such as a cartel, usually illegal.

clashcards.front: D1 Market structures — informal collusion
clashcards.back: Tacit cooperation without an open agreement, for example following a price leader.

clashcards.front: D1 Market structures — price competition
clashcards.back: Firms compete mainly by lowering prices or offering discounts.

clashcards.front: D1 Market structures — non-price competition
clashcards.back: Firms compete through branding, quality, service, advertising or product features.

clashcards.front: D1 Market structures — efficiency
clashcards.back: How well firms use resources; oligopoly can be efficient through scale but may waste resources through market power.

clashcards.front: D1 Market structures — interdependence
clashcards.back: Each firm’s decisions depend on expected reactions from rival firms.

clashcards.front: D1 Market structures — kinked demand curve model
clashcards.back: A model explaining price rigidity in oligopoly because rivals react differently to price rises and cuts.

clashcards.front: D1 Market structures — game theory
clashcards.back: Analysis of strategic decision-making where each firm considers rivals’ likely responses.

clashcards.front: D1 Market structures — real-life industries
clashcards.back: Many real markets fit monopolistic competition better than pure theoretical models.

clashcards.front: D1 Market structures — short-run monopoly position
clashcards.back: In the short run, differentiated products can give firms some price-making power and profit.

clashcards.front: D1 Market structures — long-run perfect competition position
clashcards.back: In the long run, entry reduces supernormal profit, similar to competitive markets.

clashcards.front: D1 Market structures — price competition
clashcards.back: Firms compete partly by changing prices, but products are differentiated.

clashcards.front: D1 Market structures — product differentiation
clashcards.back: Firms make their product appear different through design, quality, branding or features.

clashcards.front: D1 Market structures — brand loyalty
clashcards.back: Consumers repeatedly buy from one brand, giving the firm some market power.

clashcards.chapter: D2 Market failure and government intervention
clashcards.front: D2 Market failure and government intervention — market failure
clashcards.back: A situation where the free market allocates resources inefficiently for society.

clashcards.chapter: D2 Market failure and government intervention
clashcards.front: D2 Market failure and government intervention — merit goods
clashcards.back: Goods society underconsumes because individuals underestimate their benefits, such as education.

clashcards.chapter: D2 Market failure and government intervention
clashcards.front: D2 Market failure and government intervention — demerit goods
clashcards.back: Goods society overconsumes because individuals underestimate their costs, such as cigarettes.

clashcards.chapter: D2 Market failure and government intervention
clashcards.front: D2 Market failure and government intervention — public goods
clashcards.back: Goods that are non-rival and non-excludable, so markets may not provide them sufficiently.

clashcards.chapter: D2 Market failure and government intervention
clashcards.front: D2 Market failure and government intervention — imperfect information
clashcards.back: Consumers or producers lack full information, causing poor decisions and inefficient outcomes.

clashcards.chapter: D2 Market failure and government intervention
clashcards.front: D2 Market failure and government intervention — inequity
clashcards.back: An unfair distribution of income, wealth or access to goods and services.

clashcards.chapter: D2 Market failure and government intervention
clashcards.front: D2 Market failure and government intervention — immobile factors of production
clashcards.back: Resources such as labour or capital cannot easily move to where they are most needed.

clashcards.chapter: D2 Market failure and government intervention
clashcards.front: D2 Market failure and government intervention — positive externalities
clashcards.back: Benefits to third parties not reflected in the market price, causing underproduction.

clashcards.chapter: D2 Market failure and government intervention
clashcards.front: D2 Market failure and government intervention — negative externalities
clashcards.back: Costs to third parties not reflected in the market price, causing overproduction.

clashcards.chapter: D2 Market failure and government intervention
clashcards.front: D2 Market failure and government intervention — third parties
clashcards.back: People affected by production or consumption despite not being directly involved in the transaction.

clashcards.chapter: D2 Market failure and government intervention
clashcards.front: D2 Market failure and government intervention — taxation
clashcards.back: A government charge that can reduce harmful production or consumption.

clashcards.chapter: D2 Market failure and government intervention
clashcards.front: D2 Market failure and government intervention — subsidies
clashcards.back: Government payments that lower costs and encourage beneficial production or consumption.

clashcards.chapter: D2 Market failure and government intervention
clashcards.front: D2 Market failure and government intervention — price controls
clashcards.back: Government-set maximum or minimum prices to influence market outcomes.

clashcards.chapter: D2 Market failure and government intervention
clashcards.front: D2 Market failure and government intervention — state provision
clashcards.back: The government directly supplies goods or services when markets underprovide them.

clashcards.chapter: D2 Market failure and government intervention
clashcards.front: D2 Market failure and government intervention — privatisation
clashcards.back: Transfer of production or ownership from the state to private firms.

clashcards.chapter: D2 Market failure and government intervention
clashcards.front: D2 Market failure and government intervention — regulation
clashcards.back: Rules or laws used to control firm or consumer behaviour.

clashcards.chapter: D2 Market failure and government intervention
clashcards.front: D2 Market failure and government intervention — deregulation
clashcards.back: Removing rules to increase competition or flexibility in a market.

clashcards.chapter: D2 Market failure and government intervention
clashcards.front: D2 Market failure and government intervention — competition policy
clashcards.back: Government action to prevent monopolies, cartels or abuse of market power.

clashcards.chapter: D2 Market failure and government intervention
clashcards.front: D2 Market failure and government intervention — government failure
clashcards.back: When government intervention worsens efficiency or creates unintended costs.

clashcards.front: D3 Labour markets — derived demand
clashcards.back: Demand for labour comes from demand for the goods and services workers produce.

clashcards.front: D3 Labour markets — marginal productivity theory
clashcards.back: Firms hire workers according to the extra output or revenue each worker adds.

clashcards.front: D3 Labour markets — elastic demand for labour
clashcards.back: Quantity of labour demanded changes strongly when wages change.

clashcards.front: D3 Labour markets — inelastic demand for labour
clashcards.back: Quantity of labour demanded changes little when wages change.

clashcards.front: D3 Labour markets — supply of labour: individual
clashcards.back: The hours or effort one worker is willing to offer at different wage rates.

clashcards.front: D3 Labour markets — supply of labour: occupation
clashcards.back: The number of workers willing and able to work in a specific job or sector.

clashcards.front: D3 Labour markets — job satisfaction
clashcards.back: Non-wage benefits from work, such as enjoyment, status, security or conditions.

clashcards.front: D3 Labour markets — opportunity cost of work
clashcards.back: The value of leisure or alternatives given up when choosing to work.

clashcards.keyword: labour supply elasticity: low-skilled vs. skilled jobs
clashcards.front: D3 Labour markets — labour supply elasticity: low-skilled vs. skilled jobs
clashcards.back: Low-skilled labour is often more elastic; skilled labour is often less elastic due to training needs.

clashcards.front: D3 Labour markets — net migration
clashcards.back: Immigration minus emigration; it changes the size and skills of labour supply.

clashcards.front: D3 Labour markets — wages
clashcards.back: The price paid for labour, usually per hour, week or month.

clashcards.front: D3 Labour markets — wage differentials
clashcards.back: Differences in wages between workers, jobs, sectors or regions.

clashcards.front: D3 Labour markets — trade unions
clashcards.back: Worker organisations that bargain for wages, conditions and rights.

clashcards.front: D3 Labour markets — labour market discrimination
clashcards.back: Unequal treatment of workers based on personal characteristics rather than productivity.

clashcards.front: D3 Labour markets — labour market imperfections
clashcards.back: Factors preventing wages and employment from adjusting efficiently.

clashcards.front: D3 Labour markets — economic inactivity
clashcards.back: People of working age who are not employed and not actively seeking work.

clashcards.front: D3 Labour markets — imperfect information
clashcards.back: Workers or firms lack full information about jobs, wages or worker quality.

clashcards.front: D3 Labour markets — skill shortages
clashcards.back: Too few workers have the skills demanded by employers.

clashcards.front: D3 Labour markets — geographical immobility
clashcards.back: Workers cannot easily move location to take available jobs.

clashcards.front: D3 Labour markets — occupational immobility
clashcards.back: Workers cannot easily switch jobs because they lack required skills or qualifications.

clashcards.front: D3 Labour markets — minimum wages
clashcards.back: A legal wage floor below which workers cannot be paid.

clashcards.front: D3 Labour markets — maximum wages
clashcards.back: A legal or agreed wage ceiling above which pay cannot rise.

clashcards.front: D3 Labour markets — living wages
clashcards.back: A wage level intended to cover basic living costs.

clashcards.front: D3 Labour markets — pensions
clashcards.back: Retirement income that can influence labour supply and retirement decisions.

clashcards.front: D3 Labour markets — changing workforce
clashcards.back: Changes in workforce size, age, skills, gender composition or migration patterns.

clashcards.front: E Principles of macroeconomics — income flows
clashcards.back: Movement of income between households, firms, government, banks and the foreign sector.

clashcards.front: E Principles of macroeconomics — injections
clashcards.back: Spending entering the circular flow: investment, government spending and exports.

clashcards.front: E Principles of macroeconomics — withdrawals
clashcards.back: Money leaving the circular flow: saving, taxation and imports.

clashcards.front: E Principles of macroeconomics — multiplier effect
clashcards.back: An initial change in spending causes a larger final change in national income.

clashcards.front: E Principles of macroeconomics — consumption
clashcards.back: Household spending on goods and services.

clashcards.front: E Principles of macroeconomics — saving
clashcards.back: Income not spent on current consumption.

clashcards.front: E Principles of macroeconomics — investment
clashcards.back: Spending by firms on capital goods that increase productive capacity.

clashcards.front: E Principles of macroeconomics — government spending
clashcards.back: Public-sector spending on goods, services and infrastructure.

clashcards.front: E Principles of macroeconomics — net export
clashcards.back: Exports minus imports; positive net exports add to aggregate demand.

clashcards.front: E Principles of macroeconomics — aggregate demand analysis: factors
clashcards.back: Analysis of total demand using factors such as consumption, investment, government spending and net exports.

clashcards.front: E Principles of macroeconomics — average propensity to consume (APC)
clashcards.back: Total consumption divided by total income.

clashcards.front: E Principles of macroeconomics — average propensity to save (APS)
clashcards.back: Total saving divided by total income.

clashcards.front: E Principles of macroeconomics — marginal propensity to consume (MPC)
clashcards.back: The fraction of extra income spent on consumption.

clashcards.front: E Principles of macroeconomics — marginal propensity to save (MPS)
clashcards.back: The fraction of extra income saved.

clashcards.front: E Principles of macroeconomics — multiplier formula
clashcards.back: Simple multiplier = 1 / MPW, or 1 / (1 - MPC) in a closed model.

clashcards.front: E Principles of macroeconomics — marginal propensity to withdraw (MPW)
clashcards.back: The fraction of extra income leaked through saving, tax or imports.

clashcards.front: E Principles of macroeconomics — aggregate supply analysis
clashcards.back: Analysis of total output firms are willing to produce at different price levels.

clashcards.front: E Principles of macroeconomics — short-run aggregate supply (SRAS)
clashcards.back: Total output firms supply in the short run when some costs are fixed.

clashcards.front: E Principles of macroeconomics — long-run aggregate supply (LRAS) curve
clashcards.back: Shows the economy’s potential output when resources are fully used.

clashcards.front: E Principles of macroeconomics — Keynesian supply curve
clashcards.back: A view of AS where output can rise without inflation when spare capacity exists.

clashcards.front: E Principles of macroeconomics — classical supply curve
clashcards.back: A view of LRAS as vertical at full-employment output.

clashcards.front: E Principles of macroeconomics — macroeconomic equilibrium
clashcards.back: The point where aggregate demand equals aggregate supply.

clashcards.front: E Principles of macroeconomics — output gaps
clashcards.back: The difference between actual output and potential output.

clashcards.front: E Principles of macroeconomics — spare capacity
clashcards.back: Unused resources that allow output to rise without strong inflationary pressure.

clashcards.keyword: shifts in AD and AS curves
clashcards.front: E Principles of macroeconomics — shifts in AD and AS curves
clashcards.back: Changes in factors other than the price level move the AD or AS curve.

clashcards.chapter: S7 A Introduction to macroeconomic objectives and policies
clashcards.front: S7 A Introduction to macroeconomic objectives and policies — economic growth
clashcards.back: An increase in real output or real GDP over time.

clashcards.chapter: S7 A Introduction to macroeconomic objectives and policies
clashcards.front: S7 A Introduction to macroeconomic objectives and policies — balanced government / national budget
clashcards.back: Government spending equals government revenue.

clashcards.chapter: S7 A Introduction to macroeconomic objectives and policies
clashcards.front: S7 A Introduction to macroeconomic objectives and policies — budget deficit
clashcards.back: Government spending is greater than government revenue.

clashcards.chapter: S7 A Introduction to macroeconomic objectives and policies
clashcards.front: S7 A Introduction to macroeconomic objectives and policies — budget surplus
clashcards.back: Government revenue is greater than government spending.

clashcards.chapter: S7 A Introduction to macroeconomic objectives and policies
clashcards.front: S7 A Introduction to macroeconomic objectives and policies — national debt
clashcards.back: The total accumulated amount the government owes.

clashcards.chapter: S7 A Introduction to macroeconomic objectives and policies
clashcards.front: S7 A Introduction to macroeconomic objectives and policies — price stability
clashcards.back: Low and stable inflation.

clashcards.chapter: S7 A Introduction to macroeconomic objectives and policies
clashcards.front: S7 A Introduction to macroeconomic objectives and policies — low unemployment
clashcards.back: A macroeconomic goal where most people willing and able to work can find jobs.

clashcards.chapter: S7 A Introduction to macroeconomic objectives and policies
clashcards.keyword: equilibrium in the balance of payments
clashcards.front: S7 A Introduction to macroeconomic objectives and policies — equilibrium in the balance of payments
clashcards.back: External payments are sustainable, without persistent large deficits or surpluses.

clashcards.chapter: S7 A Introduction to macroeconomic objectives and policies
clashcards.front: S7 A Introduction to macroeconomic objectives and policies — equal distribution of income
clashcards.back: Income is shared more fairly across the population.

clashcards.chapter: S7 A Introduction to macroeconomic objectives and policies
clashcards.front: S7 A Introduction to macroeconomic objectives and policies — sustainability
clashcards.back: Economic activity meets current needs without damaging future living standards.

clashcards.chapter: S7 A Introduction to macroeconomic objectives and policies
clashcards.front: S7 A Introduction to macroeconomic objectives and policies — economic stability
clashcards.back: Avoiding large fluctuations in growth, inflation, employment and output.

clashcards.chapter: S7 A Introduction to macroeconomic objectives and policies
clashcards.front: S7 A Introduction to macroeconomic objectives and policies — improving productivity
clashcards.back: Increasing output per unit of input, such as output per worker.

clashcards.chapter: S7 A Introduction to macroeconomic objectives and policies
clashcards.front: S7 A Introduction to macroeconomic objectives and policies — rate of economic growth
clashcards.back: The percentage increase in real GDP over a period.

clashcards.chapter: S7 A Introduction to macroeconomic objectives and policies
clashcards.front: S7 A Introduction to macroeconomic objectives and policies — rate of inflation
clashcards.back: The percentage increase in the general price level over a period.

clashcards.chapter: S7 A Introduction to macroeconomic objectives and policies
clashcards.front: S7 A Introduction to macroeconomic objectives and policies — level of unemployment
clashcards.back: The number or percentage of people unemployed in the labour force.

clashcards.chapter: S7 A Introduction to macroeconomic objectives and policies
clashcards.keyword: state of the balance of payments
clashcards.front: S7 A Introduction to macroeconomic objectives and policies — state of the balance of payments
clashcards.back: The overall condition of a country’s transactions with the rest of the world.
